scope_plain: Every voter in Colorado's 2nd Congressional District, which includes all of Boulder County and stretches west along I-70 and north to Fort Collins
office_explainer: Boulder's one seat in the U.S. House. Votes on federal laws, taxes and spending.
why_it_matters: Rep. Joe Neguse has held the seat since 2019 and was unopposed in the June Democratic primary. CPR calls the district heavily left-leaning and Neguse a safe incumbent.

candidates.name: Joe Neguse
candidates.background: Lafayette Democrat; has represented the district since 2019 and is Colorado's first Black U.S. congressman (CPR). Unopposed in the June primary.

own_words.text: Says that as "a son of immigrants" he believes "we must do more to expand that dream for generations to come."
Points to his work on consumer protections and ethics laws, public schools and public lands, and to his role as an impeachment prosecutor.

candidates.name: Kelley Anne Dennison
candidates.background: 27-year-old massage therapist from Larimer County; won the June Republican primary with about 58% over Christina Blunt. CPR says her platform focuses on environmental conservation and immigration.

own_words.text: The top concern she hears is "the economy and the overall direction of the country."
"I absolutely support participating in in-person town halls and taking unscreened questions from constituents."
On federal aid to Colorado: "Disaster assistance and essential federal support should never be politicized."

candidates.name: Gaylon Kent
candidates.background: Libertarian nominee. Navy veteran and past commander of an American Legion post; ran for Congress in 2012 and U.S. Senate in 2014 (his iVoterGuide profile). Did not return the Denver Post questionnaire.

own_words.text: We deserve an America at peace.
It’s time for a flat tax and a one-page income tax return.
We have executed innocent people. It is time to abolish the death penalty.

office: Regent of the University of Colorado
scope_plain: Every voter in Congressional District 2, which includes all of Boulder County
office_explainer: One of nine elected regents who govern the University of Colorado system: tuition, budgets, the president.
why_it_matters: Open seat: Democratic regent Callie Rennison did not run again. CU Boulder is the only CU campus in this district. Regents serve six-year terms, two terms at most.

candidates.name: Marty Neilson
candidates.background: Republican nominee; unopposed in the June primary.

own_words.text: Reduce dependence on federal grants by expanding partnerships with industry, philanthropy, foundations, and state-supported innovation programs.
Lists his priorities as a safe, high-quality and affordable education for students and helping pass a College Sports Act.

candidates.name: Edie Hooton
candidates.background: Boulder resident since 1997. State representative for House District 10 (Boulder, Gunbarrel, CU Boulder) from 2017 to 2023, where she chaired the committee that decides state construction for higher education. Won a three-way Democratic primary with about 43%.

own_words.text: Wants to prioritize affordable tuition for in-state students and improve retention and graduation rates.
Says her six years in the legislature give her a strong grasp of higher-education policy, government budgeting and state politics.

candidates.name: Richard Friend
candidates.background: Libertarian nominee. Retired utility worker from Evergreen with welding and nuclear power station training; says he has no political experience (Denver Post questionnaire). No campaign site found.

own_words.text: Too much spending on sports and not enough on education and not enough diversity in thought
Says his priorities are reducing government waste, increasing productivity and guiding more effective budgets.

candidates.background: Represented Senate District 15 from 2018 to 2022. Has worked in restaurants for 35 years (Colorado Politics).

own_words.text: "Cost of living is by far the biggest complaint when I meet with voters across the district."

candidates.background: State senator since 2023. An engineer and former middle school teacher who served on her local school board (Colorado Politics).

own_words.text: "Colorado needs strong guardrails for large-scale data centers before they expand further."
Would ease the budget gap by adjusting the TABOR limit to track Medicaid cost growth, and wants more starter homes, condos and townhomes.

scope_plain: Voters in RTD Director District O, which covers Boulder, Niwot, Superior, Louisville and Boulder County west of Boulder (per the district description at a candidate forum). Check your ballot.
office_explainer: One of 15 directors who run RTD: bus and rail routes, fares, budget. Nonpartisan.
why_it_matters: Open seat: longtime District O director Lynn Guissinger is not on the ballot. Both candidates are Democrats, but the race is nonpartisan. Both talk about train service to Boulder, reliability and safety. Four-year term.

candidates.name: Jack Rosenthal
candidates.background: Software engineer who worked at Google in Boulder for six years; daily RTD rider and transit advocate who says he helped pass RTD policies and the state Transit Access Bill.

own_words.text: Running because "I am tired of the generation of leadership at RTD that has failed us."
Wants to "build the train" to Boulder and "restore reliable service."
Says RTD's technology is outdated, citing broken live bus tracking: "I'd be the only technologist on the board."

candidates.name: Audrey DeBarros
candidates.background: Executive director of Commuting Solutions, a nonprofit coalition of nine local governments and employers that advocates for transportation in the northwest metro area. Lives in Louisville; 25 years in Boulder County.

own_words.text: Top rider problems: "safety, first and foremost, reliability, frequency, access and service for everyday living."
"People will not ride RTD if they do not feel safe." Wants RTD's police force funded at least at current levels.
Points to her work on the US 36 Express Lanes, Flatiron Flyer bus rapid transit and the Highway 119 project.

office_explainer: Leads City Council meetings and is one of nine council votes; a hired city manager runs daily operations.
why_it_matters: Ranked choice: rank up to six. If no one has more than 50% of first choices, the last-place candidate is dropped and those ballots count for their next choice, until someone has a majority. Don't skip a column or give two people the same rank. Mayor Aaron Brockett faces five challengers, including Councilmember Taishya Adams; the clearest divide is the $400 million bond (2K). The mayor's pay rises to about $51,000 a year in December.

candidates.name: Lisa Ann Jacobs
candidates.background: Little biographical or campaign information is public; Boulder Reporting Lab has not published a full profile. Not using city matching funds.

own_words.text: Did not respond to Boulder Reporting Lab's questionnaire.
Boulder Reporting Lab lists her among the candidates who oppose the $400 million bond (2K).

candidates.name: Taishya Adams
candidates.background: City councilmember for nearly three years; she gives up her council seat either way. Founder of the Mukuyu Collective, an environmental consultancy; inaugural member of the city's Police Oversight Panel. Age 52; rents in South Boulder. Using city matching funds.

own_words.text: Bonds are "the best strategy to fund major facility needs," but "the current package lacks community trust and support." Told BRL she'd vote no on 2K.
"I do not support the use of automated license plate readers at this time."
Goal for year one: a "two year participatory budgeting process" that weighs water supply in every decision.

candidates.name: Aaron Brockett
candidates.background: Mayor since 2021 (chosen by council, then won Boulder's first direct mayoral election in 2023); councilmember from 2015 and Planning Board member before that. Previously ran a software firm. Age 53; owns a home in North Boulder. This would be his last term. Using city matching funds.

own_words.text: "We need to catch up on the facility backlog." If 2K fails, "we'll need to go back to the drawing board." Told BRL he'd vote yes on 2K.
On license plate readers: "I wouldn't end them unilaterally"; backs a community conversation in early 2027 on whether to keep them.
Supports more housing along transit corridors and annexing the Area III Planning Reserve for middle-income ownership homes.

candidates.name: Jameson (Jamo) Goldstein
candidates.background: CU Boulder philosophy student, age 21; grew up in Arvada; has worked as a swim coach and in educational software sales. First-time candidate. Not using city matching funds.

own_words.text: "I oppose the $400 million bond as currently presented." Wants an independent, project-by-project audit of the backlog first.
"I would end Boulder's Flock automated license plate reader contract."
Proposes a tiered tax on corporations owning more than 75 Boulder rental units to fund rent assistance.

candidates.name: Grateful Fred Instead
candidates.background: Certified by the city under the name Fred Smith; Boulder Reporting Lab lists his occupation as laborer. Not using city matching funds.

own_words.text: Did not respond to Boulder Reporting Lab's questionnaire.
Boulder Reporting Lab lists him among the candidates who oppose the $400 million bond (2K).

candidates.name: Aquiles La Grave
candidates.background: Tech entrepreneur (co-founder of Bars.com); first-time candidate. Served on Louisville's Historic Preservation Commission and BVSD's Bond Oversight Committee, and helped organize the petition behind Question 200. Came from Venezuela as a teen; U.S. citizen since 2022. Age 47. Not using city matching funds.

own_words.text: Proposes "an independent performance audit function under the direct supervision of Council." Told BRL he'd vote no on 2K.
Would put license plate readers "on hold until council creates specific policies" on data use.
For downtown: "Provide free parking in its public garages for the first two hours," plus faster permits.
